messages.content: I've been putting on a brave face for my parents but honestly I'm terrified and I don't know how to tell them.

That takes a lot of strength to recognize — and a lot of energy to keep up. You don't have to protect your parents from knowing you're scared. Most of the time, they already sense it, and giving them the chance to actually be there for you can help both of you. You don't have to have the perfect words. Something like 'I'm more scared than I've been letting on' is enough to open the door. If talking directly to them feels too hard, a nurse, a social worker, or one of the Child Life specialists here can help you find the words or even be in the room when you have that conversation. You're allowed to need support too.
I feel like everyone knows what's going on with me except me. Nobody explains anything directly.

That's a legitimate frustration, and you're right to name it. You are the patient — you have every right to understand what's happening with your own body, in clear language, not just fragments between people who assume someone else explained it. A good starting point is being direct with your doctor or nurse: 'I need you to walk me through my situation from the beginning, like I'm hearing it for the first time.' You can also ask them to slow down or repeat things. If you find it's still not happening, Patient Relations at Children's Hospital LHSC can help ensure your communication needs are being met. You don't have to accept being kept in the dark.
I hate that I have to ask permission for everything. I'm not a little kid.

That feeling of lost autonomy is one of the hardest parts of being hospitalized as a teenager — and it's completely valid. You're at an age where independence matters, and a lot of hospital routines don't account for that. Where you do have choices, take them: what you wear, when you sleep if it's flexible, who's in the room during examinations. For the things that feel like they require permission, it's worth asking your care team which decisions are actually yours to make. In Ontario, older teens have a growing set of rights around medical decisions. Knowing where you do have agency can make the things you can't control feel a bit more manageable.
My friends are posting stuff online and I'm stuck here missing everything. I feel like my whole life is passing me by.

That feeling is real and it's hard — watching everyone else continue normally while your world has been put on pause. FOMO is difficult enough outside the hospital; inside it can feel especially isolating. A few things that help some people: staying connected in smaller ways (a text, a voice note, even just reacting to things) without the pressure of explaining everything; letting one trusted friend be your link to that world rather than trying to keep up with everything; and being honest with yourself that you're not missing your life — you're dealing with something important that takes priority right now, even when that's unfair. The Paediatric Family Resource Centre on B1 also has resources to help with keeping up with school and social connection.
I keep thinking about what happens if the treatment doesn't work. Is it okay to think about that?

Yes — it's completely okay, and honestly it would be more unusual not to. When you're in a situation like this, your mind naturally goes to the worst-case scenarios as a way of trying to prepare. Thinking about it doesn't make it more likely to happen. What matters is what you do with those thoughts — whether they're something you're carrying alone or something you can say out loud to someone you trust. Your care team includes people whose specific job is to support you emotionally through exactly this kind of fear. You don't have to pretend you're only thinking about the positive outcomes. Being honest about the scary thoughts is often what makes them a little less consuming.
I'm embarrassed about some of the things the doctors have to do to me. Is that normal?

Very much so — feeling embarrassed or self-conscious about examinations and procedures is one of the most common things teenagers experience in hospital, and your care team has seen it a thousand times without judgment. You're allowed to ask for privacy during any examination: to have the door fully closed, to have only the people who absolutely need to be there in the room, and to have non-essential people step out. If having a doctor of a specific gender makes you more comfortable, you can request that too. Your comfort and dignity are taken seriously here, and there's nothing wrong with advocating for what you need.
I don't want to talk to the counselor. I just want someone to actually listen to me without writing stuff down.

That's a really clear thing to know about yourself, and it's worth telling someone. You can say exactly that to a nurse or a Child Life specialist: 'I don't want to be assessed or documented right now — I just need someone to listen.' Child Life specialists in particular are trained for exactly that kind of presence, and their conversations aren't part of your formal medical record. You can also be honest with any counselor who comes to see you: if you're not ready or not in the right headspace, saying 'I'm not up for this today' is completely within your rights.
I feel guilty that my family is spending so much money because of me being here.

That kind of guilt says a lot about how much you care about your family — but it's putting weight on you that shouldn't be yours to carry. Your being here isn't a choice you made, and your health is not a burden they resent. If financial stress is real for your family, there are social workers at Children's Hospital who can help connect your family to financial assistance programs, social supports, and resources specifically for families in this situation. It might help to talk to a social worker directly — not to fix it yourself, but to know that systems exist for this so your family doesn't have to navigate it alone.
I've been here so long I don't even know what day it is anymore.

Losing track of time is genuinely disorienting, and it happens to a lot of people in hospital — the routines blur, every day looks the same, and the outside world starts to feel distant. A few small things can help re-anchor you: keeping your phone's date visible, asking a nurse or family member to recap what day it is when they come in, or even keeping a simple note in your phone about what's happening each day. It also helps to have something to look forward to, even small — a visit, a show, a specific meal. If you're finding that the time loss is connected to your mood feeling very low or flat, that's worth mentioning to your care team.
My roommate keeps having visitors and I haven't had any in three days.

Three days without visitors is genuinely hard, especially when you can see other people getting that support right next to you. It's okay to feel lonely about that — that's a human response, not a complaint. A few options: if there are people who want to visit but haven't organized it, a nurse can help coordinate visiting logistics. If family or friends are far away, video calls are a real alternative and your nurse can help you find a private space for that. The Child Life team can also spend time with you during visits if you want company that isn't about your medical situation. You don't have to just wait it out.
What's the difference between a resident and a regular doctor?

Both are fully qualified medical doctors — the difference is experience level. A resident is a doctor who graduated from medical school and is now doing their specialty training, which typically takes several years. They work under the supervision of attending physicians, who are fully licensed specialists with completed training. At a teaching hospital like Children's Hospital LHSC, you'll often see both. Residents are real doctors making real decisions, but they're in a learning environment with oversight. If you want to know who's making decisions about your care, it's completely fair to ask: 'Who is the attending physician responsible for my treatment?'
Is everything I tell the doctors confidential or do they tell my parents?

In Ontario, the rules around confidentiality for minors depend on age and the nature of the information. Generally, doctors are expected to involve parents in the care of younger teenagers, but as you get older — and especially for sensitive topics like mental health, sexual health, or substance use — healthcare providers may keep certain conversations confidential if sharing them could harm your wellbeing or if you're considered capable of making that decision yourself. The best approach is to ask your doctor or nurse directly at the start of a conversation: 'What will you share with my parents and what stays between us?' That way you know before you say anything.
How do I actually get someone to explain my test results in plain English?

You have the right to receive information about your own health in a way you can understand. When results come back, you can specifically ask: 'Can you explain what this means in plain language?' If you still don't understand after the explanation, it's okay to say 'I'm still not following — can you try again differently?' Some people find it helpful to ask for something written down. If you're finding that conversations keep going over your head, ask if there's a patient educator or navigator available, or ask for a longer appointment time specifically for explanation. You shouldn't have to piece together your own diagnosis from fragments.
Can I refuse a procedure if I don't want it done?

Yes — informed consent matters, and you have a voice in decisions about your care. In practice, whether a minor can refuse treatment independently depends on age, the nature of the procedure, and the legal framework in Ontario. For non-emergency procedures, your care team must explain what it involves, why they're recommending it, and what happens if it's not done — and you're entitled to ask questions and say you need more time. If you're opposed to something, express it clearly to your doctor and ask what the alternatives are. For major decisions, a social worker or patient advocate can also help make sure your perspective is heard.
Is there somewhere I can actually be alone for a bit, like a quiet room or something?

Yes. Children's Hospital has quiet spaces and family resource areas where you can have some privacy. The Paediatric Family Resource Centre on B1 is one option. You can also ask your nurse if there's a quiet room on the unit you could use for a bit — many units have them. If you're in a shared room and need privacy, ask about whether a private room is available, or at minimum ask for your curtain to stay closed. Needing time to yourself is a completely legitimate request, especially if you've been in a shared space for a while.
Do the nurses change every shift? How do I make sure the new ones know what's going on with me?

Yes, nurses typically work 8- or 12-hour shifts and hand over to a new nurse at the end of each one. The handover process is structured — nurses do a detailed briefing with the incoming nurse and review your chart together. You can also ask to be included in the bedside handover so you hear the update directly and can correct anything that's been missed or add something important. If a new nurse comes in and seems unfamiliar with your situation, it's okay to say 'I want to make sure you know about X before we start' — that's self-advocacy, not being difficult.
I looked up my diagnosis online and now I'm more confused than before. Who do I ask about this?

Online information about medical conditions is almost always written for the average adult and covers every possible scenario, including the worst ones — which makes it easy to end up more scared and confused than you need to be. The right person to ask is your attending physician, because they know your specific case, not the general case. Write down the specific things you read that confused or worried you and bring the list to your next conversation. Starting with 'I was looking things up and I have some questions' is a completely reasonable opening. Asking your doctor to walk through what does and doesn't apply to you is a much more useful exercise than searching alone.
Can I get copies of my medical records?

Yes. Patients and their families have the right to access medical records. At Children's Hospital LHSC, you can make a formal records request through the Health Information Management department. Depending on your age and the nature of the records, the request may need to be made jointly with a parent or guardian. The process isn't immediate — there's a formal request and typically a processing period — but it is your right. If you want a summary of your current situation rather than a full records request, asking your care team for a written summary of your diagnosis and treatment plan is often faster.
What does it actually mean when they say I'm being monitored overnight?

Overnight monitoring means your vital signs — things like heart rate, oxygen levels, and sometimes blood pressure — are being tracked continuously or at regular intervals while you sleep. Depending on your situation, this might involve sensors clipped or stuck to your body that send data to a screen at the nurses' station, where someone checks it regularly. It doesn't mean someone is staring at you all night — it means the data is being collected so the team can see trends and catch anything unusual early. If you're not sure what specific things are being monitored for you, ask your nurse: 'What are you watching for?' That usually gives you a clearer picture.
Is there anything for older teens to do here besides watch TV?

Yes, though it depends on your mobility. The Paediatric Family Resource Centre on B1 has resources for patients and families. Child Life specialists work with older teens too — they can bring activities, help you access games, or just talk. If you have specific things you'd normally do (drawing, music, reading, gaming), most of those can come to you or be arranged. Some units also have common areas. If you're finding the days very long, telling your nurse or a Child Life specialist directly — 'I'm going stir crazy and need something to do' — is a totally legitimate thing to say and they'll try to help.
My phone is my main way of managing my anxiety. Is there any rule about using it at night?

There's no hospital-wide rule against using your phone at night. The general consideration is keeping noise low if you're in a shared room. If using your phone — whether for music, meditation apps, messaging, or just something to focus on — helps you manage anxiety, that's a legitimate reason and worth mentioning to your care team. They may have additional suggestions, but they're not going to take your coping tool away. If the anxiety itself is significantly affecting your sleep or wellbeing, that's also worth raising as something to address directly — there are supports available specifically for that.
My medication schedule at home is different from what they're giving me here. Should I say something?

Yes, definitely say something — this is important. When you're admitted, your care team reviews your home medications and may adjust timing, dose, or delivery method for clinical reasons. But they can also make mistakes or miss something. If you're noticing a difference that doesn't have an explanation you've been given, bring it up with your nurse or physician directly: 'At home I take X at Y time — can you tell me why it's different here?' Medication reconciliation is a standard part of hospital care, and your input as the person who knows your own regimen is valuable.
I need to exercise every day or I can't sleep. That's not possible here.

It might be more possible than you think, depending on your mobility and what your care team allows. Ask your nurse or doctor what physical activity is appropriate for your current situation. For many patients, walking the hallway, gentle stretching, or bodyweight movements in the room are permitted and even encouraged. A physiotherapist can also be consulted to suggest safe activity options given your specific condition. It's worth being direct: 'Exercise is important to my mental health and sleep — what can I do while I'm here?' That framing usually gets a more helpful response than asking if you're 'allowed' to move.
I want to shower in the morning but the nurse comes around really early. Can I tell them not to come in during that time?

Yes — establishing a routine that works for you is a reasonable ask. Let your nurse know at the start of their shift or the night before: 'I like to shower in the morning around X time — can you plan around that if possible?' Many aspects of morning rounds can be slightly flexible. The ones that can't be moved are usually time-sensitive medications or monitoring, and your nurse can tell you which those are. For everything else, there's often more flexibility than it might seem. Communicating your preferences doesn't make you difficult; it helps the team schedule around you.
I need to take my own medication at a specific time every day. How does that work here?

When you're admitted, you should disclose all medications you take at home — including the timing and dosage. Your care team will review them and either continue them, adjust them, or provide hospital equivalents. If a specific timing is medically important (like a medication that needs to be taken with food at a consistent time, or a hormonal medication), note that explicitly so it's flagged. Once you're admitted, medications at Children's Hospital are administered by nurses on schedule, but that schedule is built around your needs. Ask your nurse: 'My home medication needs to be given at X time for [reason] — how do we handle that here?'
Is there a curfew for when visitors have to leave?

Yes, visiting hours are structured at Children's Hospital, though parents and legal guardians generally have more flexibility than other visitors. The specific times vary by unit, and the current rules can change based on what's happening on the ward. Ask your nurse what the visiting hours are for your specific unit and what exceptions exist. If a particular visit matters to you — a friend who can only come at an unusual time, for example — it's worth asking whether an exception is possible rather than assuming it isn't. Many units are reasonably accommodating when there's a clear reason.
Can I order food from outside if the hospital menu doesn't work for me?

Depending on your diet restrictions and your care team's guidance, outside food is sometimes possible. If you're on a medically prescribed diet, anything from outside needs to be compatible with it — check with your nurse or dietitian first. If there are no dietary restrictions and the hospital menu just doesn't appeal to you, families often bring food in. Delivery to the hospital is technically possible but can be complicated — having family pick it up and bring it is more reliable. Let your nurse know what you need and they can tell you exactly what's allowed in your situation.
I'm in a shared room and my roommate is making it really hard to rest.

That's a legitimate concern — rest is genuinely part of your recovery. Start by telling your nurse specifically what the issue is: noise, lighting, visitor times, something else. Nurses can often mediate or adjust visiting schedules to make shared rooms more manageable. If the situation is significantly affecting your ability to recover, ask directly whether a private room is available. Private rooms are sometimes allocated based on clinical need, so framing it as an impact on your health and sleep gives your team something to work with. You're not being unreasonable for needing conditions where you can actually rest.
I need to pray at specific times every day. How does that work here?

Religious and spiritual practices are respected at Children's Hospital. There's a chapel and spiritual care team available to all patients. For prayer at specific times, let your nurse know your schedule — they can plan around it where possible so you're not interrupted or called for something during those times. If you need a quiet private space, your nurse can help find one or arrange for privacy in your room. There's also a chaplain available who works with patients of all faiths and no faith — they can help connect you with specific supports if needed.
I don't want anyone to visit me. How do I make that actually happen?

You can make this official. Talk to your nurse and ask to have a 'no visitors' note placed on your room — this gives staff something to point to rather than putting you in the position of turning people away yourself. You can make exceptions for specific people (like one parent) while excluding others. Your privacy is taken seriously and you don't have to justify why you don't want visitors. If specific people are persisting despite being told, that escalates to a more formal conversation with the unit, but a simple documented preference is usually enough to handle it.
Nobody has actually explained the procedure step by step. I keep getting the vague version.

That's a legitimate frustration and it's worth pushing back on. You're entitled to a detailed explanation, not just reassurance. Before any procedure, your care team is required to go through informed consent, which means explaining exactly what will happen, step by step, what you might feel, how long it takes, and what the risks are. If you haven't gotten that, ask for a specific conversation: 'Can someone walk me through exactly what is going to happen during this, from start to finish, before we do it?' You can also ask for written materials or ask if there's a video or diagram that shows the procedure. You shouldn't be going in blind.
How long does anaesthesia usually take to wear off? I have a thing I really need to be lucid for.

The timeline for feeling fully alert after general anaesthesia varies — most people feel reasonably awake within a few hours, but full mental clarity can take anywhere from a few hours to a day depending on the anaesthetic used, how long the procedure was, and individual factors. The grogginess, foggy thinking, and sometimes difficulty concentrating are normal in the immediate recovery window. Tell your anaesthesiologist and care team specifically about what you need to be alert for and when — they can factor that into how they manage your anaesthesia and recovery plan. Being clear about your priorities helps them make better decisions.
What does recovery look like after this kind of surgery — like, realistically, not the optimistic version.

That's a fair thing to ask for. Recovery timelines given by care teams are often best-case estimates, and the reality for most people involves more discomfort, fatigue, and slower progress than the optimistic version suggests. A realistic conversation includes: what pain levels to expect and for how long, what activity restrictions apply, how long before you can return to school or normal routine, what signs of complication to watch for, and when 'still feeling rough' crosses into 'call someone.' Ask your surgeon specifically for the realistic range rather than the ideal outcome — something like 'What does recovery look like for someone who has a harder time with it?' usually gets you a more honest answer.
I've heard the medication I'm being given can have some serious side effects. How do I know what to watch for?

Asking this directly is exactly the right move. Your care team should have gone through the common and serious side effects of your medication as part of your consent, but if they haven't been specific enough, ask: 'What side effects should I actually watch for, and which ones mean I need to call someone immediately?' There's usually a tiered answer — some effects are uncomfortable but expected, some mean you should mention it at your next appointment, and some mean you stop the medication and contact the team right away. Getting clarity on which category is which means you're not guessing. You can also ask your pharmacist, who is often very detailed about this.
What happens between when they discharge me and when I actually feel normal again?

That gap is real and it's worth planning for. Discharge means you're stable enough to recover outside the hospital, not that you've recovered. Depending on what you've been through, you might still be managing pain, fatigue, physical limitations, medication schedules, and the emotional aftermath of the whole experience. Your discharge paperwork should outline what to expect, what to do and not do, and who to call if something comes up. Ask specifically: 'What should I expect in the first week home?' and 'At what point should I be worried and call?' Also ask about follow-up appointments before you leave — don't wait until you're home to figure out next steps.
The consent form had a lot of risks listed. How common are those actually?

Consent forms are legally required to list all known risks, which means they include both common and very rare complications together — which can make the list look scarier than the actual picture. The way to interpret a consent form is to ask your doctor to walk through the specific risks with context: roughly how likely each one is, whether the risk applies to your specific situation, and what they would do if it happened. A one-in-a-thousand risk is very different from a one-in-ten risk but both appear on the form. You're entitled to that conversation before you sign anything.
I've had this test before at a different hospital and it was done differently. Which way is right?

Different hospitals and different care teams can have legitimate variations in how they perform the same test — different equipment, protocols, or patient preferences can all play a role. Neither way is necessarily 'right' or 'wrong.' What matters is the clinical outcome. If you're worried that a difference in procedure means something might be missed or done incorrectly, raise it directly: 'At my previous hospital they did this a specific way — can you explain why yours is different?' That's a fair question and your team should be able to explain their approach. If you remain concerned, asking for a second opinion is also within your rights.
What's the realistic timeline from diagnosis to treatment starting? Nobody's given me specifics.

Timelines vary significantly depending on the condition, the required workup, and the treatment type — which is why you keep getting vague answers. But 'I don't know exactly' is different from not telling you anything. Ask your care team specifically: 'What needs to happen before treatment starts, and what is your estimate for each step?' That breaks the timeline into pieces you can track. Also ask what factors could cause delays. If you're being transferred to a specialist, ask when that referral is going and what the expected wait is. You're entitled to a plan with milestones, not just 'we're working on it.'
Is it common to not remember anything from the surgery or is that just something that happens sometimes?

Not remembering the surgery itself is completely normal — that's the intended effect of general anaesthesia. You're not supposed to have conscious awareness during the procedure, and in the vast majority of cases, you won't. What's less common but can happen is not remembering parts of the time right before going under or right after waking up. This is usually due to the medication's effect on memory consolidation and is not a cause for concern. If you experienced something specific you're worried about — like awareness during the procedure — that's worth discussing with your anaesthesiologist directly, as it's rare but taken seriously when it occurs.
What does 'under observation' actually mean in practice? Are they watching me constantly?

Being 'under observation' means your vital signs and condition are being monitored regularly, but it doesn't mean someone is watching you every moment. In practice, it usually means sensors attached to you are sending data to a monitor at the nurses' station, nurses are checking on you at set intervals, and any changes in your readings trigger an alert. The frequency and type of observation depends on your specific situation. If you want to know exactly what's being monitored for you and how often someone will be checking in, just ask your nurse — they can walk you through the specific plan.
There have been three different doctors who've come in separately and said slightly different things. Who's actually in charge of my care?

That's a fair question and a sign you need clearer communication. In a hospital like LHSC, you typically have an attending physician who is the responsible physician for your overall care — they're the one accountable for your treatment plan. The others might be specialists, residents, or fellows, each focusing on a specific aspect. Ask your nurse or the next doctor who comes in: 'Who is the most responsible physician for my care?' That person should be the one giving you the bottom line. If information from different people seems contradictory, it's also fair to ask for a team meeting so you're getting one consistent message.
Someone called a 'social worker' wants to meet with me. What are they actually there for?

A hospital social worker works with patients and families on non-medical aspects of care — things like emotional support, family dynamics, financial stress, housing, school, discharge planning, and connecting you with community resources. They're not there because something is wrong with how you're coping; they're part of routine care for many patients, especially those with longer stays. You can talk to them about things that have nothing to do with your medical diagnosis — like how the experience is affecting your mental health, your relationships, or practical concerns about what happens when you go home. The conversation is confidential within professional limits.
What's the difference between a specialist and a consultant — are those the same thing?

In Canadian hospital practice, the terms are often used interchangeably. A specialist is a physician who has done additional training in a specific area of medicine — cardiology, oncology, neurology, and so on. When they're 'consulted' on your case by your primary team, they're called in as a consultant. So a consultant is a specialist being asked for their expert input. If a consultant comes to see you, they're usually focused on one specific aspect of your care, not your overall situation. Your most responsible physician is still the one overseeing everything.
There was a person who sat with me for an hour and just talked. They weren't a doctor. What was their role?

That sounds like a Child Life specialist, a social worker, or possibly a chaplain or spiritual care provider — all of whom offer support that isn't clinical in the medical sense. Child Life specialists focus on emotional wellbeing and coping for patients of all ages, including teens. They're specifically trained to just be present and supportive without an agenda. If you found that helpful and want to see them again, ask your nurse who came to see you — they'll be able to look it up and arrange another visit. Knowing who it was also lets you ask for them by name next time.
I want to talk to someone about how all of this is affecting me mentally, not physically. Who do I ask for?

Ask your nurse or doctor for a referral to the social work or psychology team — most paediatric hospitals have both. A social worker can provide immediate support and connect you with resources. A psychologist or psychiatrist can provide more structured mental health support if that's what's needed. You can also ask for a Child Life specialist, who works with teens specifically on the emotional side of hospitalization. You don't need to be in crisis to ask for this — ongoing stress, anxiety, low mood, or just needing someone to talk to are all valid reasons. Asking for mental health support is taking your recovery seriously.
Can I request a specific nurse if I felt more comfortable with one of them?

You can make the request, yes. Speak to the charge nurse on your unit — they're the one who does the scheduling. Explain that you felt particularly comfortable with a specific nurse and ask if they can be assigned to you when they're working. This isn't always possible (nurses work specific shifts, units have complex staffing) but it's a reasonable request and many units try to accommodate it. Even if you can't always have that nurse, knowing there's someone you connect with can make the other shifts easier. It's worth asking.
Who's actually responsible for making sure all the different departments treating me are on the same page?

Formally, that's the most responsible physician — usually an attending physician or in some cases a hospitalist — whose job includes coordinating the overall care plan across specialties. In practice, the coordination between departments can have gaps, which is why it matters for you and your family to be active participants. Ask at each visit: 'Has this been shared with my other team?' and at rounds: 'Is everyone aligned on the plan?' If you feel like important information is getting lost between departments, raise it with your care team or ask for a case conference where all the relevant people get together. Patient Relations can also help if coordination is genuinely falling short.
What's the role of the person who came to talk to me about going home and what happens after?

That's likely a discharge planner or a member of the care coordination or transitions team. Their job is specifically to plan what happens when you leave the hospital — making sure you have what you need at home, that follow-up appointments are booked, that any home care or equipment is arranged, and that you and your family understand what to do. It's one of the most important conversations you'll have because what happens in the first days and weeks after discharge significantly affects your recovery. If you have specific concerns about going home — support at home, getting back to school, physical limitations — that person is the right one to raise them with.
I've been dealing with a lot of different people. Is there one main person I should be directing my questions to?

For medical questions — diagnosis, treatment, prognosis, procedures — the most responsible physician is your main point of contact. For day-to-day needs and coordination, your bedside nurse is usually the most responsive. For anything about emotions, coping, or practical life issues, the social worker or Child Life specialist. For problems with how things are being handled, Patient Relations. The system isn't perfectly streamlined, but knowing those four lanes helps. You can also ask your nurse: 'Who's the best person to ask about X?' and they'll usually route you correctly. You don't have to figure out the org chart on your own.
A medical student asked if they could observe my examination. Did I have to say yes?

No. Participating in the education of medical students is voluntary. You have the right to decline, and doing so will not affect the quality of your care in any way. If you said yes and now feel uncomfortable, you can change your mind at any time. If saying no directly feels awkward, you can simply say 'I'd prefer not to have observers today' and leave it at that — you don't owe an explanation. Some people are comfortable being part of teaching; some aren't. Both are completely valid.
